common_name: America Peony (Gold Medal Single Brilliant Red Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil, or set out potted plants in spring; America won the American Peony Society's Gold Medal for its brilliant, true red single flowers.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, and be patient the first year or two while the plant establishes before flowering heavily. America bears large, single, brilliant true-red flowers with a prominent center of golden stamens, a clean, uncomplicated flower form that lets the intensity of the red color stand out more than a fully double bloom would. It won the American Peony Society's Gold Medal and remains a benchmark red single peony, prized both in the garden and for cutting since single-form peonies hold up well in a vase without shattering as quickly as heavier doubles. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover, and avoid planting too deeply, since peonies set shallowly bloom far more reliably than those buried too far below the soil surface.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

common_name: Buckeye Belle Peony (Semi-Double Dark Red Early-Blooming Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil, or set out potted plants in spring; Buckeye Belle is an American Peony Society award winner known for its very early, dark garnet-red bloom.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, and be patient the first year or two while the plant establishes before flowering heavily. Buckeye Belle bears semi-double flowers of a deep, dark garnet-red with a satiny sheen, opening among the earliest peonies to bloom each spring and extending the cut-flower and garden display season before the classic midseason doubles take over. Its sturdy stems hold the relatively compact flowers upright well without staking in most gardens. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover, and site in a spot with good air circulation to minimize the risk of botrytis blight on the dark-colored petals.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil, or set out potted plants in spring; Raspberry Sundae is named for its two-tone, dessert-like color combination.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, and be patient the first year or two while the plant establishes before flowering heavily. Raspberry Sundae bears large bomb-form flowers with an outer ring of rose-pink guard petals surrounding a mounded center of creamy-white to pale yellow petaloids, a color layering that gives the bloom the look of its dessert namesake. It flowers in midseason on sturdy stems well suited to cutting, filling out a vase display with both color and heavy fragrance. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover, and stake or grow through a peony ring if the large flower heads weigh down the stems after rain.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil, or set out potted plants in spring; Sorbet bears richly fragrant, layered bomb-form flowers popular for both garden display and cutting.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, and be patient the first year or two while the plant establishes before flowering heavily. Sorbet produces bomb-form flowers with soft pink outer guard petals surrounding a dense, ruffled center that fades toward cream, a blended color effect combined with a strong, sweet fragrance that makes it a favorite for cut arrangements. Its compact stature keeps stems relatively sturdy under the weight of the full blooms compared with some larger-flowered doubles. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover, and divide congested clumps only when flowering declines, since peonies can be left undisturbed for decades once established.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

common_name: Mrs. Franklin D. Roosevelt Peony (Classic Double Pink Heirloom Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil, or set out potted plants in spring; a mid-twentieth-century introduction still grown as a dependable heirloom pink double.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, and be patient the first year or two while the plant establishes before flowering heavily. Mrs. Franklin D. Roosevelt bears large, full double flowers in a clear, warm pink, opening in midseason on a vigorous, floriferous plant that has kept it in circulation as a reliable heirloom cultivar for well over half a century. Its heavy bloom and classic double form make it a dependable choice for cutting as well as garden display, filling out a spring border with the fragrance typical of old double lactiflora peonies. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover, and stake heavy flower heads if they begin to flop after rain.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

common_name: Alexander Fleming Peony (Classic Fragrant Double Lavender-Pink Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil, or set out potted plants in spring; a long-popular Dutch-bred double peony grown for its heavy, richly fragrant bloom.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, and be patient the first year or two while the plant establishes before flowering heavily. Alexander Fleming bears large, very full, rounded double flowers in a soft lavender-pink with a strong, sweet fragrance, opening in midseason on a vigorous and reliably floriferous plant that has made it a long-standing favorite for both cut-flower production and garden display. The dense, heavy blooms often need staking or a peony ring to keep them upright once fully open, especially after rain. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover, and give it full sun for the strongest stems and best flower production.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil, or set out potted plants in spring; Etched Salmon bears an unusual warm salmon-pink color uncommon among peony cultivars.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, and be patient the first year or two while the plant establishes before flowering heavily. Etched Salmon bears Japanese-form flowers with broad outer guard petals in a warm salmon-pink surrounding a center of narrow, ruffled staminodes in a paler blended tone, a softer and less common color than the more typical pinks, whites, and reds of most peony cultivars. The single-layer guard petals give the flower a lighter, more open look than a fully double bloom while still providing plenty of garden presence in midseason. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover, and plant in full sun for the truest color development.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

common_name: White Cap Peony (Japanese-Form Red Peony with Cream Center)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil, or set out potted plants in spring; White Cap pairs deep red guard petals with a contrasting cream-white center for strong two-tone impact.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, and be patient the first year or two while the plant establishes before flowering heavily. White Cap bears Japanese-form flowers with broad, deep red outer guard petals surrounding a mounded center of narrow, cream-to-white staminodes, a bold two-tone combination that reads clearly even from a distance in a mixed spring border. The relatively open, single-layer guard petal form sheds rain more easily than dense double peonies, which helps stems stay upright through spring storms. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover, and site in full sun with good air movement for the strongest color contrast and healthiest foliage.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

common_name: Pink Hawaiian Coral Peony (Early-Blooming Fragrant Semi-Double Coral-Pink Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall with eyes facing up and covered by no more than two inches of soil, or set out potted plants in spring; one of the earliest-blooming peonies in the Coral series, extending the peony season ahead of most midseason cultivars.

directions: Set divisions shallowly in early fall in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, and be patient the first year or two while the plant establishes before flowering heavily. Pink Hawaiian Coral bears semi-double, bright coral-pink flowers with a light fragrance, opening among the earliest peonies each spring, related to the well-known Coral Charm and Coral Sunset cultivars but with its own distinct warm pink cast. The relatively open flower form and sturdy stems hold up well without staking in most garden situations. Deadhead spent blooms and cut foliage to the ground in fall to reduce disease carryover, and expect the coral coloring to soften somewhat as each flower ages, a normal trait shared across this coral-toned breeding line.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach
